NIST SP 800-160 Vol 1 Rev 1 | Appendix H.10 Transition
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-3 Configuration Change Control

questionsV2.question: Finance wants the 900 retired SlimLine units sold to a refurbisher. Which step MOST directly addresses the disposal risk the security lead must sign off?

options.A: A contract clause making the refurbisher liable for any data recovered from the units.
options.B: Removing each unit from the asset inventory once the refurbisher confirms collection.
options.C: Sanitizing every storage component to a level matched to the data it held, with verification recorded.
options.D: Physically destroying the encrypting PIN pad in each unit before the units leave the site.

questionsV2.explanation: A retired terminal is a filing cabinet on wheels: card data, logs, keys, configuration and whatever a technician once copied to it locally. NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 MP-6 Media Sanitization requires media to be sanitized before disposal, release out of organizational control or release for reuse, using defined techniques and procedures, and SR-12 Component Disposal, new in Rev 5, extends that to the component itself. SP 800-160 Vol 1 Rev 1 Appendix H.14 Disposal is the lifecycle process, which includes removing information and deactivating accesses and dependencies. NIST SP 800-88 is the guide that decides between clear, purge and destroy; cite it without pinning a revision, because Revision 1 was withdrawn on 26 September 2025 and superseded by Revision 2. A is the right control for a different problem, moving liability rather than removing data. B is wrong phase, a records step that follows sanitization and would otherwise erase the bank's own account of what left. D is wrong scope, treating one component while the customer data sits on the terminal's storage. Sanitize to the data, not to the device.
questionsV2.recallLine: Retired terminals are being sold to a refurbisher. What most directly addresses the disposal risk?

optionsShort.B: Retire units from the asset inventory
optionsShort.C: Sanitize storage to the data's level, verified

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: What should the contract say about the refurbisher's obligations once sanitized units leave the bank?

B.label: wrong phase
B.wouldAnswer: What records step closes out an asset after it has been sanitized and collected?

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: What is required for the one component that holds cryptographic keys under the card brand rules?

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | MP-6 Media Sanitization; SR-12 Component Disposal; SI-12(3) Information Disposal
NIST SP 800-160 Vol 1 Rev 1 | Appendix H.14 Disposal
NIST SP 800-88 (revision not pinned: Rev 1 withdrawn 2025-09-26, superseded by Rev 2)

questionsV2.question: The console is reachable from any office workstation and from the technicians' home connections. Which change BEST treats the console itself, rather than its accounts, as the protected asset?

options.A: Requiring a second authentication factor from every technician who signs in to the console.
options.B: Reviewing the console's account list each quarter and removing accounts no longer needed.
options.C: Admitting console sessions through one managed access point that mediates and records them.
options.D: Encrypting console session traffic so credentials cannot be read on the office network.

questionsV2.explanation: Accounts and systems are different asset classes and they fail differently. Everything in options A, B and D improves who may hold a credential or what happens to it in flight, and none of them changes the fact that the console answers from anywhere. NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 AC-17(3) Remote Access | Managed Access Control Points requires remote access to be routed through a defined number of managed network access control points, and AC-3 Access Enforcement puts the enforcement in the system rather than at its edge. A single mediated path is also the only arrangement that produces one place to watch. A is the right control for a different problem, strengthening the authentication event the stem deliberately sets aside. B is detective when preventive is asked, finding a stale account a quarter after it stopped being needed. D is wrong scope, protecting the traffic rather than the set of places the system will answer. Ask what the asset is before choosing the control.
questionsV2.recallLine: An administration console answers from anywhere. What treats the console, not its accounts, as the asset?

optionsShort.C: One managed access point for sessions

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: What raises the cost of using a technician's stolen password?

B.label: detective when preventive is asked
B.wouldAnswer: How does QuickCash find accounts that outlived the person or the job?

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: What stops someone on the office network reading a console session in transit?

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-17(3) Remote Access | Managed Access Control Points
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-3 Access Enforcement

questionsV2.question: The technicians need administrative rights on the console only while a work order is open. Which arrangement BEST matches that need?

options.A: Granting the privilege when a work order opens and removing it automatically when the order closes.
options.B: Issuing each technician a second, privileged account used solely for administrative work.
options.C: Granting standing administrative rights and requiring a supervisor to approve each console session.
options.D: Storing the privileged credential in a vault that technicians check out and check back in.

questionsV2.explanation: The entitlement, not the credential, is what an attacker eventually inherits, so the question is how long it exists. NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 AC-2(6) Account Management | Dynamic Privilege Management is the mechanism: privileges are adjusted at runtime rather than held statically, and AC-2(2) Automated Temporary and Emergency Account Management requires temporary and emergency accounts to be removed or disabled automatically after a defined period. AC-6(5) Privileged Accounts restricts who may hold them at all. Worth knowing for the exam and for a vendor conversation: the phrase just-in-time access does not appear in SP 800-53 Rev 5 at all. The source that uses the term is the CISA Zero Trust Maturity Model 2.0, Section 5.1 Identity, whose Access Management function reaches its Optimal stage when automation authorizes just-in-time and just-enough access. B is the right control for a different problem, separating privileged from routine use while the privilege stays permanent. C is symptom not cause, adding a gate in front of rights that are never withdrawn. D is wrong scope, controlling custody of a secret rather than the life of the entitlement behind it. Shorten the grant, not just the queue in front of it.
questionsV2.recallLine: Technicians need admin rights only while a work order is open. Which arrangement matches that need?

optionsShort.A: Grant on work order, revoke on close

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: How should routine work be kept off an account that holds administrative rights?

C.label: symptom not cause
C.wouldAnswer: What adds oversight when a privilege genuinely has to be held continuously?

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: How is a shared or emergency credential kept out of five people's notebooks?

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-2(6) Dynamic Privilege Management; AC-2(2) Automated Temporary and Emergency Account Management; AC-6(5) Privileged Accounts
CISA Zero Trust Maturity Model 2.0 | Section 5.1 Identity, Access Management function

questionsV2.question: QuickCash wants staff to sign in to the two cloud applications with their existing directory accounts, and the directory will stay in the regional office. Which element MOST determines whether that federation is trustworthy?

options.A: Whether the identity provider runs on the firm's own hardware or on a hosted platform.
options.B: Whether the assertion travels over a channel encrypted end to end between the parties.
options.C: Whether each application can read the full set of attributes held in the directory.
options.D: Whether the terms each party is trusted for are agreed and documented before the first sign-in.

questionsV2.explanation: Federation is a transfer of belief, and what makes it safe is that both sides have written down what they are believing. NIST SP 800-63C-4 Section 3.5 Trust Agreements states that all federation transactions shall be governed by the terms of one or more trust agreements between the applicable parties, and it enumerates the relationships those terms cover, including what the relying party trusts the identity provider to represent and what the identity provider trusts the relying party to do with the attributes released. Section 3.2 defines the roles the agreement binds. One useful caution: SP 800-63C-4's own two models are general-purpose identity providers and subscriber-controlled wallets, at Section 3.1. The on-premise, cloud and hybrid split is the exam outline's deployment framing, and the trust-agreement obligation is identical wherever the provider runs. A is symptom not cause, because location decides who operates the provider, not whether the trust was ever established. B is the right control for a different problem: a well-protected assertion from an untrusted issuer is still untrusted. C is wrong scope, one clause inside the agreement and, released in full, a bad one. Write down what you are trusting.
questionsV2.recallLine: Staff will sign in to cloud applications using an on-premises directory. What most determines trustworthiness?

A.label: symptom not cause
A.wouldAnswer: What changes about operational responsibility when an identity provider moves to a hosted platform?

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: What protects an assertion from disclosure or tampering while it is in transit?

C.label: wrong scope
C.wouldAnswer: What should a trust agreement say about which attributes may be released to which relying party?

sources: NIST SP 800-63C-4 | Section 3.5 Trust Agreements; Section 3.2 Roles; Section 3.1 Federation Models
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | IA-8 Identification and Authentication (Non-Organizational Users); SA-9 External System Services

questionsV2.question: Board members will keep directory accounts while contractors are created only in the cloud tenant, so two identity stores will authenticate to the same applications. Which control MOST directly addresses the risk that creates?

options.A: Requiring both stores to sign assertions with the same algorithm and key length.
options.B: Reconciling the two stores against one authoritative person record during every access review.
options.C: Applying the directory's password policy to the cloud tenant so the two stores match.
options.D: Requiring multi-factor authentication in both stores before either issues an assertion.

questionsV2.explanation: Two authoritative sources for the same population means one human being can hold two identities, and each store's review sees only its own half. That is how a contractor who becomes an employee keeps a set of rights nobody remembers granting, and it is the failure QuickCash already had once under a different name. NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 IA-4 Identifier Management requires identifiers to be assigned under authorization and managed so they are not reused, and AC-2 Account Management requires accounts to be reviewed for compliance with account management requirements on a defined frequency. Reconciliation to one person record is what makes either of those checks meaningful across two stores. A is the right control for a different problem, assertion integrity. C is symptom not cause, aligning a parameter while leaving the identifier space unreconciled. D is correct but not first, because a duplicate identity that authenticates strongly is still a duplicate identity. Count people, then count accounts.
questionsV2.recallLine: Two identity stores authenticate the same population to the same applications. Which control addresses that?

optionsShort.A: Same signing algorithm in both stores
optionsShort.B: Reconcile both stores to one person record

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: What keeps an assertion from being forged or replayed against a relying party?

C.label: symptom not cause
C.wouldAnswer: How does the firm keep authentication strength consistent for staff wherever their account lives?

D.label: correct but not first
D.wouldAnswer: What raises the cost of using a stolen contractor password against either store?

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | IA-4 Identifier Management; AC-2 Account Management
NIST SP 800-63C-4 | Section 3.4 Federated Identifiers

questionsV2.question: QuickCash's card-data extract is copied nightly from the console to an analyst's laptop, then into a spreadsheet on a shared drive. Access is controlled separately on each of the three systems. Which control BEST protects the information itself as it moves?

options.A: Requiring the same group membership on all three systems before access is granted.
options.B: Encrypting each system's storage so the extract is unreadable if a disk is removed.
options.C: Labelling the extract and enforcing flow rules that follow the label between systems.
options.D: Reviewing the three systems' access lists on the same quarterly cycle.

questionsV2.explanation: Three well-controlled systems can still add up to an uncontrolled dataset, because the extract loses its protection at every boundary and reacquires whatever the next system happens to grant. NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 AC-4 Information Flow Enforcement requires approved authorizations to be enforced for controlling the flow of information within the system and between connected systems, and AC-16 Security and Privacy Attributes provides the binding that makes it possible, associating attributes with information and enforcing decisions on the basis of them. Together they are the catalogue's answer to information as an access-control asset class, distinct from the system-by-system enforcement in AC-3. A is wrong scope, harmonizing three per-system decisions while the data still crosses unattended. B is the right control for a different problem, protecting media at rest rather than a copy in motion. D is detective when preventive is asked, and it looks at who may reach each system rather than where the data went. Control the data, not only the doors.
questionsV2.recallLine: A card-data extract crosses three separately controlled systems. What protects the information itself?

optionsShort.A: Same groups on all three systems
optionsShort.C: Label the data, enforce flow rules

A.label: wrong scope
A.wouldAnswer: How does the firm keep one person's entitlements consistent across three systems?

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: What protects the extract if a laptop or a drive leaves the building?

D.label: detective when preventive is asked
D.wouldAnswer: How does the firm confirm periodically that only the right people can reach each system?

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-4 Information Flow Enforcement; AC-16 Security and Privacy Attributes
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-3 Access Enforcement

questionsV2.question: Legal's draft reply threatens action under the terms of service. What should the security lead advise FIRST?

options.A: Ask the researcher to sign a non-disclosure agreement before the report is examined.
options.B: Establish a published reporting channel with safe-harbour terms, then reply through it.
options.C: Refer the report to the card brands so they can direct FinCorp's response to it.
options.D: Reproduce the finding and patch it before any reply is sent to the researcher.

questionsV2.explanation: FinCorp has no route by which a report can arrive, so every reply it drafts is improvised, and improvised replies from Legal are how a ninety-day deadline becomes a press cycle. NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 RA-5(11) Vulnerability Monitoring and Scanning | Public Disclosure Program is the precise and rarely quoted control: establish a public reporting channel for receiving reports of vulnerabilities in organizational systems and system components. NIST SP 800-218 RV.1.3 states the developer-side obligation, a policy addressing vulnerability disclosure and remediation with the roles and processes to support it. NIST SP 800-216 is the dedicated federal guideline on the subject. A is the right control for a different problem, since a non-disclosure agreement manages a paid engagement, not an unsolicited report from someone who owes FinCorp nothing. C is not the decision-maker's; FinCorp owns the system and the reply. D is correct but not first, because the clock runs whether or not anyone answers, and a silent patch invites publication. Build the channel, then use it.
questionsV2.recallLine: A researcher reports a live flaw and Legal drafts a threat. What should the security lead advise first?

optionsShort.B: Publish a channel with safe harbour
optionsShort.C: Refer it to the card brands

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: What governs confidentiality when FinCorp commissions a penetration test from a firm it pays?

C.label: not the decision-maker's
C.wouldAnswer: Who must be told once the scope of a cardholder-data exposure is established?

D.label: correct but not first
D.wouldAnswer: What does FinCorp owe its customers once a reported flaw has been confirmed?

NIST SP 800-218 | RV.1.3 vulnerability disclosure and remediation policy
NIST SP 800-216 named as the dedicated federal disclosure guideline

questionsV2.question: The finding is reproduced. The VP of Engineering proposes shipping the fix in the release already scheduled for eleven weeks out. Which response BEST reflects how remediation should be decided?

options.A: Ship in the scheduled release, because unscheduled changes carry risks of their own.
options.B: Ship immediately, because any confirmed defect in a money path is an emergency.
options.C: Ask the researcher whether she will extend the ninety-day deadline to cover the release.
options.D: Rank it against the other open findings by exploitability and impact, then set the date.

questionsV2.explanation: Remediation timing is a risk decision, and a risk decision needs a basis that survives being asked about later. NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 CA-5 Plan of Action and Milestones requires documented planned remediation actions to correct weaknesses noted during control assessments, with milestones, and RA-7 Risk Response requires the organization to respond to findings in accordance with its own risk tolerance. NIST SP 800-115 Chapter 8, Post-Testing Activities, covers turning findings into mitigation recommendations and a remediation plan. Ranking is what lets FinCorp defend either a rushed fix or a scheduled one. A is not the decision-maker's, treating schedule ownership as though it settled a risk question. B is correct but not first: urgency is very likely the right conclusion here, and it is still a conclusion rather than the method the question asks for. C is the right control for a different problem, because the researcher's clock is not FinCorp's risk basis. Decide by risk, then argue about the calendar.
questionsV2.recallLine: When should a confirmed money-path defect be fixed, and on what basis is that decided?

A.label: not the decision-maker's
A.wouldAnswer: Who owns the release calendar, and what does that ownership actually decide?

B.label: correct but not first
B.wouldAnswer: What is the likely outcome once this finding has been ranked against the others?

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: What is worth discussing with a researcher when a fix genuinely cannot be delivered in ninety days?

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | CA-5 Plan of Action and Milestones; RA-7 Risk Response
NIST SP 800-115 | Chapter 8 Post-Testing Activities

questionsV2.question: One mitigation cannot ship for six months because a payment partner's interface must change first. Which record BEST handles that gap?

options.A: A dated exception naming the risk accepted, the compensating measure and the approver.
options.B: A note in the release backlog explaining why the change is currently blocked.
options.C: An entry in the risk register listing the partner as an external dependency.
options.D: A revised finding severity reflecting how hard the flaw turns out to be to exploit.

questionsV2.explanation: A gap that nobody has accepted is a gap that nobody owns, and six months later the only question anyone asks is who agreed to it. NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 CA-5 Plan of Action and Milestones is where the unfinished remediation lives, with its milestones and its owner. NIST SP 800-53B, Chapter 2, supplies the other half: where a control cannot be implemented as written, a compensating control providing equivalent protection may be substituted with documented justification. NIST SP 800-37 Rev 2 Chapter 3 places the acceptance itself at the AUTHORIZE step, where a named official accepts residual risk rather than the risk simply persisting. B is symptom not cause, recording the blockage and not the acceptance. C is wrong scope; the dependency is real and the record the stem needs is the decision about it. D is the right control for a different problem, because rescoring changes the number and leaves the accountability unassigned. Somebody signs, and the signature has a date on it.
questionsV2.recallLine: A mitigation is blocked for six months by a partner. Which record handles the gap properly?

B.label: symptom not cause
B.wouldAnswer: How does the engineering team track why a queued change has not moved?

C.label: wrong scope
C.wouldAnswer: Where does FinCorp record that a partner's timetable can hold up its own remediation generally?

D.label: right control, wrong problem
D.wouldAnswer: What should change if new evidence shows the flaw is far harder to exploit than first assessed?

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | CA-5 Plan of Action and Milestones
NIST SP 800-53B | Chapter 2, compensating controls with documented justification
NIST SP 800-37 Rev 2 | Chapter 3, AUTHORIZE step and risk acceptance

questionsV2.question: The team wants one test technique that would have caught both the negative amount and the sixteen-decimal amount before release. Which is MOST likely to have found them?

options.A: Functional test cases derived from the deposit feature's acceptance criteria.
options.B: Interface testing exercising each parameter the deposit endpoint accepts.
options.C: Misuse cases written from how an attacker would abuse the deposit flow.
options.D: Coverage analysis showing which lines of the balance service were executed.

questionsV2.explanation: Both defects sit in the space between what the feature was asked to do and what it will actually accept, and only one technique on this list is designed to explore that space on purpose. A misuse case starts from an actor with hostile intent and asks what they would send, which is how somebody types a minus sign or sixteen decimals before a customer does. NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 SA-11 Developer Testing and Evaluation requires a developer test and evaluation plan and the evidence of its execution, and SI-10 Information Input Validation is the control the defects violate. NIST SP 800-218 PW.5.1 names input validation and output encoding as the canonical secure-coding practice. OWASP Top 10:2025 files this family under A06 Insecure Design. A is wrong scope, derived from what the feature should do, and nobody writes deposit minus one hundred as an acceptance criterion. B is the right control for a different problem, checking that each parameter is handled rather than that the handling is safe when abused. D is symptom not cause, reporting that lines ran rather than that they behaved. Test what you do not want to happen.
questionsV2.recallLine: Which technique would have caught a negative deposit and a sixteen-decimal amount before release?

A.label: wrong scope
A.wouldAnswer: What confirms the deposit feature does what the business asked it to do?

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: What confirms every documented parameter of the endpoint is accepted and handled?

D.label: symptom not cause
D.wouldAnswer: How does the team find code paths that no test has ever executed?

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | SA-11 Developer Testing and Evaluation; SI-10 Information Input Validation
NIST SP 800-218 | PW.5.1 secure coding, validate all inputs
OWASP Top 10:2025 | A06 Insecure Design

questionsV2.question: The examiner wants evidence that the pipeline enforces the bank's rules rather than merely documenting them. Which approach BEST produces that evidence?

options.A: A quarterly audit sampling merged changes against the written development standard.
options.B: A checklist each team lead signs before a release is promoted into production.
options.C: Policy expressed as machine-checked pipeline rules that fail the build and record the result.
options.D: A dashboard showing how many findings each team closed in the most recent release.

questionsV2.explanation: An examiner asking for enforcement is asking for something that cannot have been skipped, and a rule that runs is the only artefact on this list with that property. It also produces its own evidence as a by-product, which is the second half of what was asked. NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 SC-50 Software-Enforced Separation and Policy Enforcement is the nearest control in the catalogue, and it is new in Revision 5; CM-6 Configuration Settings governs the settings the rules assert. NIST SP 800-218 PO.3.3 requires the toolchain to be configured to generate artifacts that support the security checks. Worth being precise: the phrase software-defined security appears in no NIST document, so SC-50 is a functional match rather than a name match, and it should be presented that way. A is detective when preventive is asked, sampling a quarter after the fact. B is symptom not cause, capturing a person's assertion rather than an enforced condition. D is the right control for a different problem, measuring remediation throughput. Evidence is what the machine produced, not what the team promised.

questionsV2.question: Any team can queue work on the shared build runners. Which risk does that arrangement MOST directly create for the Cardless Cash release?

options.A: One team's build step can read another team's secrets or artefacts.
options.B: Builds will queue behind each other and the weekly release will slip.
options.C: Teams will adopt different build tools and the artefacts will diverge.
options.D: The runners will fall behind on operating-system patches between releases.

questionsV2.explanation: A build runner is a machine that holds every credential its jobs need and every artefact they produce, and a shared runner holds all of them at once. A job is arbitrary code by definition, so the team that queues it inherits whatever the runner can reach, and the vault the bank has just bought does not help once a job can ask the vault on someone else's behalf. NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 AC-6 Least Privilege, SC-2 Separation of System and User Functionality, and SC-4 Information in Shared System Resources are the controls that name this class of exposure; note that SC-2's Revision 4 title was Application Partitioning. NIST SP 800-218 PO.5 requires environments involved in software development to be separated and protected. B is the right control for a different problem, a capacity concern rather than a security one. C is wrong scope, a consistency issue between teams rather than a boundary failure inside one runner. D is correct but not first, a real maintenance gap that shared queueing did not cause. Ask what the runner can reach.

questionsV2.question: Every developer can push directly to the main branch of the private repository. Which control BEST addresses the exposure that creates?

options.A: Scanning the repository's history for secrets committed before the vault existed.
options.B: Requiring commits to be signed so each change can be attributed to a developer.
options.C: Restricting repository read access to the three teams that work on it.
options.D: Requiring an independent review and a passing check before a change enters main.

questionsV2.explanation: The last incident began with one developer's decision reaching production with nobody in between, and a repository where anyone can push to main reproduces exactly that condition inside a private repository instead of a public one. NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 CM-3 Configuration Change Control requires proposed changes to be reviewed and approved or disapproved with explicit consideration of security and privacy impact analyses, and AC-5 Separation of Duties is why the reviewer is somebody else. NIST SP 800-218 adds the software-specific half: PS.1 protects all forms of code from unauthorized access and tampering, and PW.7 covers reviewing or analysing human-readable code before release. A is wrong phase, cleaning up history without governing what enters main next. B is detective when preventive is asked, producing attribution after the change has landed. C is wrong scope, narrowing who can read rather than who can change. A gate on the branch is the control; everything else describes the branch.

questionsV2.question: The rebuilt API will issue short-lived tokens instead of a master key. Which additional check MOST directly addresses the failure that let attackers read any account?

options.A: Rate limiting each token so a caller cannot enumerate accounts quickly.
options.B: Verifying on every request that the token's subject owns the record requested.
options.C: Rotating the token signing key on a schedule the managed vault enforces.
options.D: Logging every API call with its token subject and the record it touched.

questionsV2.explanation: Short-lived tokens fix who is calling. The original failure was that the API never asked whether the caller was entitled to the object it named, so any authenticated caller could read any account, and a token with a fifteen-minute lifetime does that just as thoroughly as a master key did. NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 AC-3 Access Enforcement requires the system to enforce approved authorizations for logical access to information, and AC-6 Least Privilege sizes what those authorizations should be. OWASP Top 10:2025 places object-level authorization failures under A01 Broken Access Control, which in the 2025 edition also absorbs server-side request forgery. A is symptom not cause, slowing the enumeration while still returning records the caller should not see. C is the right control for a different problem, protecting the token's integrity rather than the decision made after it is validated. D is detective when preventive is asked. Authentication says who; authorization has to say what, and every request needs both.

optionsShort.D: Log every call and record touched

D.wouldAnswer: How does the bank reconstruct which records an abusive caller reached?

questionsV2.question: Management asks which change would have stopped the technician's downloaded tool from running at all. Which control BEST meets that description?

options.A: Anti-malware configured to submit unknown executables to the vendor for analysis.
options.B: A policy forbidding technicians from downloading software to fleet machines.
options.C: Blocking the fleet's outbound web access to sites known to host hacking tools.
options.D: A deny-by-default policy admitting software the organization has explicitly authorized to execute.

questionsV2.explanation: Every option except D starts from a list of things known to be bad, and a diagnostic tool downloaded that morning is on nobody's list. NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 CM-7(5) Least Functionality | Authorized Software - Allow-by-Exception is the precise control: identify the software authorized to execute, employ a deny-all permit-by-exception policy to allow it, and review and update the list on a defined frequency. Its sibling CM-7(4) Unauthorized Software - Deny-by-Exception is the weaker direction, and the catalogue says so by structure. Note the vocabulary: Rev 5 uses allow-list and deny-list where older material says whitelisting and blacklisting. A is detective when preventive is asked, and it acts on an executable that is unknown by definition. B is the right control for a different problem, a rule aimed at a person rather than a condition enforced on the machine. C is wrong scope, applying deny-by-exception to the network, where the list can never be complete and the tool arrived on a technician's own laptop anyway. Enumerate the good, not the bad.

questionsV2.question: The analyst finds that the Toledo machine's local log now begins after the second reboot. Which change would MOST improve the company's ability to investigate the next report?

options.A: Extending local log retention on every machine from thirty days to one year.
options.B: Forwarding events to a separate repository as they are written, with synchronized time.
options.C: Requiring technicians to file a written report after every maintenance visit.
options.D: Configuring anti-malware to write its detections into the machine's Windows event log.

questionsV2.explanation: A record that lives only on the machine it describes is a record the machine can lose, and here two reboots were enough. NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 AU-9(2) Protection of Audit Information | Store on Separate Physical Systems or Components requires audit records to be stored on a system or component physically different from the one being audited, which is the whole answer to this failure. AU-4 Audit Log Storage Capacity, AU-11 Audit Record Retention, and AU-8 Time Stamps with SC-45 System Time Synchronization make the collected records usable across 5,000 machines, and AU-6(3) Correlate Audit Record Repositories is what turns them into a timeline. NIST SP 800-92 is the dedicated log-management guide; the requirement above does not depend on it. A is symptom not cause, treating the age of a record while leaving it in the only place it can be destroyed. C is the right control for a different problem, an administrative account of a visit rather than machine evidence. D is wrong scope, enriching one source on the same host that loses everything. Get the record off the box.

questionsV2.question: Analysts confirm unauthorized code on four machines and cannot yet say how it arrived. Management wants the fleet protected today. Which action BEST fits mitigation at this point?

options.A: Reimaging the four machines from the standard build and returning them to service.
options.B: Opening a change request to add allow-listing across the fleet at the next window.
options.C: Isolating the four machines from the management network while the fleet stays monitored.
options.D: Notifying the card brands and the state regulator that a compromise has been confirmed.

questionsV2.explanation: Mitigation is the act of stopping the incident from getting larger while the question of how it started is still open, and isolation is the only option here that does that without destroying the answer. NIST SP 800-61 Rev 3 places this in the Respond Function, where RS.MI-01 covers incidents being contained and RS.MI-02 covers eradication. NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 supplies the mechanism in IR-4 Incident Handling, IR-4(2) Dynamic Reconfiguration, and SC-7(20) Boundary Protection | Dynamic Isolation and Segregation. One structural note worth carrying: Revision 2 of SP 800-61 grouped containment, eradication and recovery into a single phase and was withdrawn on 3 April 2025; Revision 3 puts containment and eradication under Respond and recovery under Recover. A is wrong phase, jumping to eradication and recovery and erasing the evidence of the entry point. B is correct but not first, the durable fix on a schedule the stem says is too slow. D is the right control for a different problem, a reporting obligation under IR-6 that protects nothing today. Contain before you clean.

questionsV2.question: Three weeks later the incident is closed. Which outcome BEST shows that the lessons-learned step actually worked?

options.A: The software policy, the maintenance contract and the response playbook were each changed.
options.B: A report was circulated describing the timeline and the root cause in full detail.
options.C: The analysts who handled the incident briefed the wider team on what they had seen.
options.D: A follow-up meeting was scheduled once recovery of the four machines was complete.

questionsV2.explanation: The test of a lessons-learned step is whether anything is different afterwards, and only A names artefacts that changed. NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 IR-4 Incident Handling states the obligation directly: incorporate lessons learned from ongoing incident handling into response procedures, training and testing, and implement the resulting changes accordingly, with IR-8 Incident Response Plan requiring the plan itself to be reviewed and updated. NIST CSF 2.0 puts the same idea in ID.IM-01 through ID.IM-04, where improvements are identified from evaluations, from tests and exercises, from operational processes, and are then reflected in the plans. NIST SP 800-61 Rev 3 adds a change of emphasis worth knowing: lessons should often be shared as soon as they are identified rather than held until recovery concludes. B is symptom not cause, documenting the incident while nothing changed. C is the right control for a different problem, moving knowledge between people rather than into procedure. D is wrong phase, and it is the habit Revision 3 argues against. Look for the diff, not the deck.

questionsV2.question: The tabletop found the plan readable. The operations director wants the next exercise to confirm that each named person can state their own steps. Which test type BEST fits?

options.A: A walkthrough in which each role reads and talks through its own procedures in sequence.
options.B: A simulation in which the team responds to an injected scenario under time pressure.
options.C: A parallel test bringing the alternate switch up beside production and comparing output.
options.D: A full interruption test failing production over to the alternate site and back.

questionsV2.explanation: The ladder the exam tests runs read-through and tabletop, then walkthrough, then simulation, then parallel, then full interruption, and each rung adds one thing. A walkthrough is the rung where the plan stops being a document the team has read and becomes procedures individuals can state for their own role. Be careful with the sourcing here: this five-type ladder is CISSP-canon vocabulary and is not NIST's taxonomy. NIST SP 800-84 uses training sessions, tabletop exercises, functional exercises and tests, and NIST SP 800-34 Rev 1 Section 3.5.3 defines a tabletop as discussion-based only, with no equipment deployed. The control obligation is NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 CP-4 Contingency Plan Testing. B is wrong phase, the next rung up, and it measures reaction rather than knowledge of the steps. C is correct but not first, committing real recovery infrastructure to procedures nobody has yet performed. D is not the decision-maker's, since the board has ruled out an outage of production. Climb one rung at a time.

questionsV2.question: The walkthrough passed. The director now wants to see whether the team decides correctly when facts arrive out of order and time is short, still without touching production. Which test type BEST fits?

options.A: A tabletop exercise, facilitated by an outside consultant against a new scenario.
options.B: A parallel test, with the alternate switch processing a copy of live traffic.
options.C: A simulation, with the team responding to injected events in a controlled environment.
options.D: A full interruption test, scheduled inside an approved maintenance window.

questionsV2.explanation: What the director is asking to measure is judgement under incomplete information, and that is exactly the rung a simulation occupies: the team performs its roles against events fed to it, in a controlled environment, without the production system being at risk. NIST SP 800-34 Rev 1 Section 3.5.3 describes the nearest NIST equivalent, the functional exercise, as personnel validating operational readiness by performing their duties in a simulated operational environment. Remember that the five-type ladder is CISSP-canon; SP 800-84's categories are training sessions, tabletop exercises, functional exercises and tests, and only tabletop is common to both vocabularies. The control obligation sits in SP 800-53 Rev 5 CP-4 with CP-4(1) Coordinate with Related Plans. A is wrong phase, a rung already cleared. B is the right control for a different problem: a parallel test proves the alternate switch computes correctly, not that people decide well. D is correct but not first, the top rung and the one that depends on all the others passing. Match the rung to the question being asked.

optionsShort.D: Full interruption in a maintenance window

questionsV2.question: The simulation stalls for fifty minutes because the only person who can authorize the failover is on a flight. Which change to the plan MOST directly addresses that?

options.A: Adding a second alternate site so the failover has more than one destination.
options.B: Naming a deputy for every plan role, with the authority each deputy may exercise.
options.C: Recording the exercise so the delay can be reviewed with the recovery team afterwards.
options.D: Moving the call tree from a printed sheet to an automated notification service.

questionsV2.explanation: A recovery plan that depends on one reachable human has a single point of failure made of flesh, and eleven people across three time zones guarantees that somebody is always unreachable. The fix is delegation recorded in advance: who stands in, and what they may decide. NIST SP 800-34 Rev 1 Section 4.2.2 Notification Procedures requires the plan to document how recovery personnel are notified during business and non-business hours, and the plan structure the document specifies carries delegation of authority alongside the team rosters. NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 CP-2 Contingency Plan requires roles, responsibilities and contact information for key personnel, with CP-3 Contingency Training behind it. A is the right control for a different problem, adding destinations when the failure was authority. C is symptom not cause, capturing the delay rather than removing it. D is correct but not first, since a faster call reaches the same absent person. Name the deputy before the flight.

questionsV2.question: Both exercises are finished. Which follow-up BEST converts them into an improvement the next real outage would feel?

options.A: Filing the two exercise reports with the evidence pack for the annual examination.
options.B: Repeating the simulation next quarter to see whether the team's timings improve.
options.C: Briefing the board on the fifty-minute delay and the reasons that produced it.
options.D: Revising the plan's authority and notification steps, then retesting those steps.

questionsV2.explanation: An exercise produces a finding, and a finding that does not change the plan is a cost with no return. NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 CP-4 Contingency Plan Testing requires the organization to review the contingency plan test results and initiate corrective actions if needed, and CP-2 Contingency Plan requires the plan to be revised to address changes and problems encountered during implementation, execution or testing. NIST CSF 2.0 ID.IM-02 makes the same point from the framework side: improvements are identified from security tests and exercises, and ID.IM-04 requires the affected plans to be updated. Retesting only the changed steps is what turns the loop closed rather than open. A is the right control for a different problem, evidence for the examiner and no change to the plan. B is wrong phase, retesting before anything has been altered. C is symptom not cause, reporting the delay upward and leaving the document as written. Change the plan, then test the change.

questionsV2.question: An analyst investigating a suspected insider at Global ATM Corp needs to establish which technician was physically at the Toledo machine on the night in question. The suspect is the administrator of the badge system, holds the account that exports its records, and has not yet been told that he is under investigation. Which step should the analyst take FIRST?

options.A: Interview the suspect's supervisor about the technician's assignment for that week.
options.B: Query the badge system directly for the day's entries and export them to a report.
options.C: Compare the badge records with the ATM's local event log on the machine itself.
options.D: Preserve the badge records from a source the suspect cannot alter, then compare.

questionsV2.explanation: An investigation into the person who administers the evidence has one problem before it has any others, and that is custody. NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 AU-9 Protection of Audit Information requires audit information and tooling to be protected from unauthorized access, modification and deletion, and its enhancements say how: AU-9(2) Store on Separate Physical Systems or Components, and AU-9(4) Access by Subset of Privileged Users, which limits management of audit functionality to a defined subset of privileged users. Those controls exist precisely so that the administrator of a system is not the custodian of the record about them. IR-4(12) Incident Handling | Malicious Code and Forensic Analysis covers the analysis that follows. NIST SP 800-86 is the guide that covers forensic technique itself. A is correct but not first, part of the investigation and no protection for an alterable record. B is symptom not cause, producing an answer from a system the suspect controls, so the answer cannot be defended later. C is wrong phase, correlating before preserving and touching the live machine to do it. Secure the record before you read it.

questionsV2.question: Global ATM Corp's cash-replenishment crews work alone at night, opening safes at unattended machines in retail car parks. After a crew member was followed and threatened at a site last month, the safety committee has asked for a way for someone under coercion to summon help without the coercer noticing anything unusual. Which measure BEST meets that requirement?

options.A: A distinct code that opens the safe normally and silently raises an alarm at dispatch.
options.B: A panic button in the service vehicle that the crew member presses before approaching.
options.C: A check-in call to dispatch on arrival at each site, logged with the arrival time.
options.D: A requirement that two crew members be present for every replenishment visit.

questionsV2.explanation: The requirement has two halves that most controls satisfy only one of: the signal must reach help, and the coerced person must appear to be complying. A duress code does both, because the safe behaves exactly as it would on a normal open while dispatch receives an alert nobody at the machine can see. Sourcing matters here and is worth stating plainly: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 contains no duress control and no travel-security control. The single occurrence of the word duress in the catalogue sits in the discussion of AC-2(6) Dynamic Privilege Management, about privileges under emergency conditions, and it is not a control. The nearest catalogue neighbours are PE-6 Monitoring Physical Access and IR-6 Incident Reporting, and the substantive requirement belongs to physical security and safety of life rather than to an information security control set. B is wrong phase, since coercion usually begins at the machine, not in the vehicle. C is detective when preventive is asked, and a coercer can stand beside the call. D is the right control for a different problem, reducing the chance rather than providing the signal. A duress signal has to look like compliance.

C.wouldAnswer: How does dispatch learn that a crew is overdue at a site?
